evidence.claim: The Tunnel of Trees follows Lake Michigan from north of Harbor Springs to Cross Village, a roughly 20-mile stretch of M-119 beneath a tree canopy.
evidence.quote: The Tunnel of Trees is a Scenic Heritage Route spanning roughly 20 miles of the M-119 highway in northern Michigan. This beautiful road follows the Lake Michigan shoreline just north of Harbor Springs to Cross Village.

evidence.claim: The road is narrow and winding, with hairpin turns and no centerline; lake views appear only occasionally.
evidence.quote: Part of the charm of the Tunnel is its tree-lined narrow roadway with hairpin turns and low hanging tree canopy.

evidence.claim: The Tunnel of Trees Scenic Heritage Route Committee says the corridor’s designation recognizes its natural beauty and the community’s commitment to protecting its integrity.
evidence.quote: The M119 Tunnel of Trees Corridor is designated a Scenic Heritage Route because of its natural beauty and because of the community's commitment to its integrity.

evidence.claim: The roadway follows an old Ottawa trail through oak, maple, birch and cedar.
evidence.quote: The roadway meanders through oaks, maples, birch and cedars along an old Ottawa trail.

evidence.claim: The numbered highway reached Cross Village in 1933, when M-131 was extended north from Harbor Springs.
evidence.quote: Until 1933, M-131 had terminated in Harbor Springs; the highway was extended to the north along Little Traverse Bay and the Lake Michigan shoreline through the community of Good Hart before terminating in Cross Village.

evidence.claim: That northern section lost its designation in 1937 and regained it in 1945.
evidence.quote: This section of highway would be stripped of its designation in 1937 and truncated back to Harbor Springs.

evidence.claim: The M-119 number replaced M-131 in 1979; the route has not changed since.
evidence.quote: The current highway was designated in 1979, replacing the former route of M-131; the routing has remained unchanged since.

evidence.claim: From Harbor Springs, Bluff Drive becomes Lake Shore Drive as M-119 turns north along the shoreline.
evidence.quote: Bluff Drive becomes Lake Shore Drive near the Harbor Point Golf Course, and M-119 turns northward to follow the Lake Michigan shoreline at the mouth of Little Traverse Bay.

evidence.claim: The highway narrows into forest, continues through Good Hart and ends in Cross Village at State Road.
evidence.quote: Along this area of the routing, the highway narrows in width and continues through the forest without a centerline most of the remainder of the way.

evidence.claim: The committee identifies Devil’s Elbow and Horseshoe Bend among the route’s landmarks, and notes that the corridor passes through properties that are almost all privately owned.
evidence.quote: Route highlights include Devil’s Elbow, Horseshoe Bend and multiple nature preserves.

evidence.claim: At Saint Ignatius in Good Hart, the white clapboard church and rows of white cemetery crosses give the village a distinct landmark.
evidence.quote: Saint Ignatius Church is a white-painted wooden structure covered with clapboard, with a tall wooden steeple. Adjacent to the church is the Middle Village Cemetery, which contains rows of white crosses marking gravesites.

evidence.claim: A Catholic chapel occupied a bark longhouse here in 1741. Its replacement, dedicated in 1833, burned on Easter Sunday in 1889.
evidence.quote: In 1741, a Roman Catholic chapel was established at this location in a bark longhouse. The first structure was replaced by a more substantial version, dedicated by Father Frederic Baraga, in 1833. That church was destroyed by fire on Easter Sunday, April 21, 1889.

evidence.claim: Construction began immediately on the present church. A local carpenter managed the work, much of it carried out by local Odawa people, and the new building was dedicated that September.
evidence.quote: Construction immediately began on the current church as a replacement. Father Servatius Altmicks from Harbor Springs hired a local carpenter to manage the construction, and much of the work was done by the local Odawa. The new church was dedicated by Rt. Reverend Bishop Richter on September 13, 1889.

evidence.claim: White crosses stand in rows beside the white clapboard church and its wooden steeple.
evidence.quote: Saint Ignatius Church is a white-painted wooden structure covered with clapboard, with a tall wooden steeple. Adjacent to the church is the Middle Village Cemetery, which contains rows of white crosses marking gravesites.

evidence.claim: At Saint Ignatius in Good Hart
evidence.quote: Saint Ignatius Church and Cemetery is a historic church and cemetery at 101 N. Lamkin Road in Good Hart, Michigan, US.

evidence.claim: M-119 ends at Cross Village, on Lake Michigan at the southern edge of Sturgeon Bay.
evidence.quote: Cross Village is located in northwestern Emmet County, on the shore of Lake Michigan at the southern limit of Sturgeon Bay.

evidence.claim: The community formed part of the Odawa settlement region known as Waganagisi, or L’Arbre Croche, extending south to Harbor Springs.
evidence.quote: L'Arbre Croche, known by the Odawa people as Waganagisi, was a large Odawa settlement in Northern Michigan.

evidence.claim: In 1836, the Odawa ceded land across much of the Eastern Upper Peninsula and Northern Lower Peninsula under the Treaty of Washington.
evidence.quote: In 1836, the Odawa gave up land across most of the Eastern Upper Peninsula and Northern Lower Peninsula when they signed the Treaty of Washington.

evidence.claim: Chief Joseph Nowimashkote then initiated a plan to buy back land at Cross Village, which was also called La Croix in the 19th century.
evidence.quote: Chief Joseph Nowimashkote initiated a plan for the Odawa to buy back their land at Cross Village, also called La Croix in the 19th century.

evidence.claim: extending south to Harbor Springs.
evidence.quote: It covered the region from Harbor Springs to Cross Village in present-day Emmet County, Michigan.
